issues.subcategory: impossible confidence interval for RMSEA
issues.description: The reported RMSEA point estimate of .03 is entirely above both bounds of its 90% confidence interval [.025, .026]. A confidence interval cannot be entirely below the point estimate it is meant to contain. Additionally, the interval is only .001 wide, which is implausibly narrow for an RMSEA estimate derived from any realistic model. This is almost certainly a typographic error (possibly intended as [.025, .035] or [.030, .036]), but as reported it is statistically impossible and undermines confidence in the reported fit statistics.

issues.subcategory: anomalously large chi-square difference statistic
issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing the cross-lagged paths between RWA→SDO (B = .02) and SDO→RWA (B = -.001) yields χ²(1) = 15,389.13. This is internally inconsistent with the other chi-square difference tests reported in the same section. Using the approximate scaling implied by the other reported tests (e.g., a path difference of .09 yielding χ²(1) = 50.98), a path difference of approximately .021 should yield χ²(1) ≈ 3–5, not 15,389. This value is approximately three orders of magnitude too large and strongly suggests an error in computation or transcription, which would invalidate the conclusion drawn from it about the directionality of the SDO–RWA relationship.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001), a finding we explore more fully in the Discussion.

issues.subcategory: confidence interval bounds equal point estimates due to rounding
issues.description: For the WILL→SDO path, the point estimate B = -.04 is identical to the lower bound of its 95% CI [-.04, -.03], meaning the estimate falls on the boundary of the interval rather than inside it. The same problem occurs for WILL→RWA: B = -.01 with CI [-.01, -.003]. While this likely reflects truncation from rounding small values to two decimal places, as reported the CIs are mathematically impossible (a point estimate cannot equal a bound of its own confidence interval). Greater precision in reporting (e.g., three decimal places) is necessary for these small coefficients.

issues.subcategory: standard deviation notation used in place of standard error
issues.description: Throughout the results section, unstandardized path coefficients are accompanied by 'SD' values (e.g., 'B = .83, SD = .01'). In the context of SEM parameter estimates, these values are standard errors (SE), not standard deviations. Standard deviations describe variability in observed data; standard errors describe the precision of parameter estimates. Mislabeling SE as SD is a consistent error that could confuse readers and misrepresents the statistical properties of the reported estimates.
issues.quote: the autoregressive path for willingness to sacrifice was strong (B = .83, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [.82, .84])

issues.subcategory: FIML misdescribed as imputation
issues.description: The paper states 'Missing data were imputed using FIML.' Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) is not an imputation technique. FIML is a direct maximum likelihood estimation method that uses all available data to estimate model parameters without creating imputed datasets. Describing it as imputation is technically incorrect and could mislead readers about how missing data were handled, particularly regarding the Missing at Random (MAR) assumption that underlies FIML but is never discussed.
issues.quote: Missing data were imputed using FIML.

issues.subcategory: traditional CLPM used instead of Random Intercept CLPM
issues.description: The authors employ a standard autoregressive cross-lagged panel model (CLPM). It is well established (e.g., Hamaker et al., 2015, Psychological Methods) that the traditional CLPM conflates stable between-person trait differences with within-person change processes. Cross-lagged coefficients in a traditional CLPM can be entirely driven by trait-like between-person covariances rather than genuine within-person temporal dynamics. Given that SDO, RWA, and environmentalism are well-documented stable dispositions (confirmed by the very high autoregressive paths reported: .79–.95), this confounding is especially severe here. The Random Intercept CLPM (RI-CLPM) partitions stable between-person variance from time-varying within-person fluctuations and is now the recommended approach for this research question. Not using it means the cross-lagged effects—the central findings of the paper—may largely reflect between-person differences rather than within-person change, fundamentally undermining causal interpretation.
issues.quote: We used cross-lagged path analysis to infer causal associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.subcategory: stationarity assumption imposed without testing
issues.description: The authors constrain all cross-lagged parameters to be time-invariant across all four measurement intervals without testing whether this assumption holds. They explicitly justify this by interest rather than empirical verification: 'we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects…and not on whether these effects change.' Stationarity is a strong assumption that can be tested by fitting an unconstrained model and comparing fit. If the effects of SDO or RWA on environmentalism change over the five-year interval (e.g., due to changing political or climatic context in New Zealand between 2009–2013), forcing them to equality produces biased pooled estimates. Failure to test this assumption cannot be justified by researcher preference and should be treated as a limitation.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.subcategory: measurement non-equivalence due to missing item at Time 2
issues.description: One RWA item was not administered at Time 2 but was present at all other waves. The authors mention this without discussing its implications. This creates structural non-equivalence in the RWA factor at Time 2 relative to all other time points: the factor has different item composition at one wave, violating the assumption of configural invariance that underpins all longitudinal measurement comparisons. The authors do not explain how the Time 2 RWA factor was specified (e.g., whether it was treated as a 5-item vs. 6-item factor, or whether the item was simply dropped from all waves), nor do they discuss whether this affects the measurement invariance constraints imposed on the model.
issues.quote: The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: two-indicator latent factor identification
issues.description: The environmentalism construct is modeled as a latent variable with only two indicators. A two-indicator factor is generally not identified in a standard CFA without additional constraints (e.g., equal loadings or equal residual variances). The authors do not explain how identification was achieved for this factor or what constraints were applied. With only two items, the factor is also highly sensitive to the specific items chosen and cannot provide reliable separation of true factor variance from item-specific variance. The authors do not address whether this under-determination affects their results.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as individual's willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] two items on sacrifice intentions

issues.subcategory: inadequate justification for accepting model with CFI = .86
issues.description: The authors dismiss CFI = .86 as an artifact of 'model complexity,' but this framing is misleading. CFI corrects for model complexity relative to the null model, and a value of .86 indicates that the proposed model accounts for only 86% of the covariance structure relative to the saturated model. Conventional thresholds require CFI ≥ .90 (minimum acceptable) or ≥ .95 (good fit). CFI of .86 indicates meaningful model misspecification that is not explained away by complexity arguments. The RMSEA and SRMR values do not compensate for this because they index different aspects of fit. The misfit may indicate that the stationary, homogeneous cross-lagged structure is an inadequate representation of the data.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.subcategory: narrow operationalization of environmentalism
issues.description: The dependent variable is operationalized as 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment' using two items. The paper's title, abstract, introduction, and discussion consistently use the broad term 'environmentalism' to describe this variable. However, environmentalism is a multidimensional construct encompassing environmental beliefs, attitudes, affect, knowledge, policy support, and behavioral intentions. Sacrifice intentions are one narrow behavioral willingness component and do not constitute environmentalism as a general construct. The introduction reviews research on climate change denial, risk perception, policy support, and concern as if they are interchangeable with the study's outcome measure, but these are distinct constructs that may relate differently to SDO and RWA. This mismatch between construct label and operationalization inflates the scope of conclusions the data can support.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as individual's willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.

issues.subcategory: conflation of distinct environmental attitude constructs
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, climate change denial, risk perception, concern for the environment, support for environmental policy, and willingness to sacrifice are used interchangeably under the umbrella of 'environmentalism.' These are conceptually and empirically distinct constructs. The introduction reviews literature across all these outcomes as though they are equivalent to the measured outcome (sacrifice intentions). The discussion makes conclusions about 'environmentalism' broadly and even invokes 'climate change denial' literature when interpreting results from a sacrifice-intention measure. This construct conflation prevents meaningful comparison with prior literature and overstates the generality of the findings.
issues.quote: SDO is related to lower environmentalism across time, and RWA was a weaker, but significant, negative predictor.

issues.subcategory: causal language unjustified by cross-lagged panel design
issues.description: The paper repeatedly uses explicit causal language despite a design (CLPM) that cannot establish causality. The methods section states the analysis is designed 'to infer causal associations'; the discussion concludes 'there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism'; and later 'this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes.' Cross-lagged panel models establish temporal precedence but cannot rule out unmeasured confounders, reverse causation at a finer timescale, or (as noted above) stable between-person trait covariances that generate spurious lagged effects. The causal framing is particularly unjustified given the authors' own acknowledgment of bidirectionality and the potential role of third variables (e.g., economic factors).
issues.quote: We used cross-lagged path analysis to infer causal associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment...These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.subcategory: motivational inference from attitudinal survey data
issues.description: The abstract and conclusion claim that 'the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority.' Motivation cannot be inferred from cross-lagged associations between self-report attitude scales. The study measures levels of agreement with attitudinal statements; it does not assess motivational processes, goals, or underlying cognitive mechanisms. This claim vastly oversteps what the data can support and represents a systematic conflation of measured attitudes with psychological motivation.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority.

issues.subcategory: discussion invokes unmeasured constructs without data support
issues.description: Several paragraphs in the discussion elaborate extensively on environmental racism, climate vulnerability of marginalized groups, IPCC inequality findings, and Social Dominants' preferences for directing environmental hazards toward low-status groups. None of these phenomena were measured in the study. The outcome variable is willingness to sacrifice for the environment; the study contains no data on exposure to environmental hazards, distribution of climate effects, or actual environmental harm. Drawing these connections from a temporal association between SDO scores and sacrifice intentions is a substantial inferential overreach that misrepresents what the data demonstrate.
issues.quote: Bryant [35] noted that environmental racism occurs when people of colour are disproportionately exposed to environmental hazards, and receive less protection from these hazards, than more privileged groups.

issues.subcategory: attrition across five waves not described
issues.description: The paper reports a total N of 22,974 but provides no information about the number of participants who completed each wave, the pattern or extent of dropout across the five years, or whether attrition was systematic (i.e., related to the study variables). FIML handles missing data under the Missing At Random (MAR) assumption, but this assumption is never stated, discussed, or evaluated. With five annual waves spanning 2009–2013, attrition in longitudinal panel studies is typically substantial. If dropout is related to SDO, RWA, or environmentalism (Missing Not At Random), FIML estimates will be biased. Readers cannot evaluate the severity of this threat without basic attrition information.
issues.quote: Of the 22,974 participants included in this study...Missing data were imputed using FIML.

issues.subcategory: measurement invariance tests not reported
issues.description: The authors describe imposing configural, metric (factor loading), scalar (intercept), and residual variance constraints across time points, but never report the results of tests evaluating whether these constraints are tenable. Standard longitudinal SEM practice requires reporting sequential invariance tests (configural → metric → scalar) with fit comparisons (e.g., ΔCFI, ΔRMSEA) to justify each level of constraint. Without these tests, it is unknown whether the observed data support the claimed measurement invariance. If scalar invariance does not hold, latent mean comparisons and cross-lagged parameters are not interpretable in the way the authors claim. This is a critical omission given the entire analytic framework depends on these constraints.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the factor loadings of our latent variables to equality so that, for each factor, the individual items that make up the factor were set to be equal across time points...Next, we constrained the means (intercepts) of the factors to equality.

issues.subcategory: which RWA scale items were used not specified
issues.description: The paper states only that six items from Altemeyer's RWA scale were used and provides one example item. Altemeyer's full RWA scale contains 30 items (or 22 in the short form), and the specific items selected have substantial consequences for the construct assessed and for comparability with other studies. Reporting which six items were selected is necessary for replication and for evaluating the content validity and reliability of this abbreviated measure. The reliabilities reported (.70) suggest that item selection may have introduced measurement issues that cannot be evaluated without knowing which items were used.
issues.quote: Right-wing authoritarianism was assessed with six items from Altemeyer's [27] RWA scale. These included items such as 'Our country will be destroyed someday if we do not smash the perversions eating away at our moral fibre and traditional beliefs'.

issues.subcategory: syntax availability contingent on acceptance
issues.description: The authors state that Mplus syntax 'will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.' Making analytic code available only upon acceptance (rather than to reviewers) prevents reviewers from verifying the analysis, checking for specification errors, and evaluating replicability. This is inconsistent with open science standards and prevents peer review from fulfilling its verification function. Given the complex model specification with multiple invariance constraints and potential identification issues for the two-indicator factor, access to the syntax is especially important.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.subcategory: no pre-registration and undisclosed analytical decisions
issues.description: The study is a secondary analysis of an existing large longitudinal dataset (the NZAVS) with no pre-registration. Multiple analyst degrees of freedom exist in this context: which time points to use, which items to include in short scales, whether to use composite or latent variable approaches, model constraints, and significance thresholds. The adoption of p < .01 as the significance threshold is attributed to a NZAVS technical document and sample size, but this decision—as well as the choice of the stationary model, the specific invariance constraints, and the decision to treat constructs as unidimensional—appear to have been made without pre-registration. The bidirectionality findings and SDO-RWA asymmetry appear exploratory but are reported without flagging them as such.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a conservative p-value threshold of p < .01 to indicate significance of findings

issues.subcategory: national representativeness overclaimed given sample composition
issues.description: The authors claim the sample is 'nationally representative' and that results are 'highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.' However, the sample is 62% female (New Zealand's population is approximately 51% female) and 86% Pākehā (New Zealand European), while the New Zealand population is approximately 70% European, with significant Māori (17%), Asian (15%), and Pacific (8%) populations. These demographic imbalances are not discussed, yet SDO and RWA have known associations with ethnicity and gender. The overrepresentation of women may systematically bias mean levels and relationships with environmentalism, as SDO and RWA exhibit gender differences. These sampling limitations are not acknowledged in the strengths and limitations section.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.subcategory: SDO dimensions not analysed despite known differential effects
issues.description: The authors cite their own prior work (Stanley et al. [24]) showing that the two dimensions of SDO—dominance-seeking and anti-egalitarianism—differentially predict environmentalism cross-sectionally, and that it is environmental attitudes that predict SDO dimensions longitudinally in student samples. Despite this, the current study uses a composite SDO score that collapses across these dimensions. The six SDO items used include three pro-dominance and three pro-equality items; how these are scored and whether they were analyzed as a single composite is not clarified. Using a composite obscures the dimensional structure that the authors themselves identify as theoretically and empirically important.
issues.quote: Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items from Sidanius and Pratto's [1] SDO6 scale. Three items favoured dominance, such as 'To get ahead in life, it is sometimes okay to step on other groups', and three favoured equality

issues.subcategory: contradiction between stated latent variable invariance and missing item
issues.description: The methods describe constraining item residual variances and factor loadings to equality across all five time points as a core model specification. However, the methods also acknowledge that one RWA item was absent at Time 2. These two claims are directly contradictory: if the factor structure differs at Time 2 (one fewer item), residual variances and loadings for the missing item cannot be constrained to equality across all time points as stated. The paper never resolves this contradiction, leaving the actual model specification unclear.
issues.quote: We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points...The item...was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: contradiction between cross-lagged results and causal conclusions given bidirectionality
issues.description: The discussion concludes that 'SDO has a stronger influence on environmental attitudes over time than the reverse,' yet the results show that the lagged effects of WILL on RWA and RWA on WILL are statistically indistinguishable (χ²(1) = 2.70, p = .100). If the bidirectional association between RWA and environmentalism is symmetrical, claiming that the flow runs primarily from ideology to environmentalism is not supported for RWA. The authors acknowledge this but then proceed to frame the overall conclusions as supporting directional causal claims from ideology to environmentalism without adequately qualifying this for RWA.
issues.quote: whilst there was no difference between the strength of the effect of RWA on environmentalism and vice versa (2(1) = 2.70, p = .100)...These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.
